title: Hosea 1:1–11
context: The LORD’s word comes to Hosea the son of Beeri, in the days of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, kings of Judah, and in the days of Jeroboam the son of Joash, king of Israel. The LORD tells Hosea to take a wife of prostitution and children of unfaithfulness, because the land commits great adultery, forsaking the LORD. Hosea takes Gomer the daughter of Diblaim, and the LORD names the children Jezreel, Lo-Ruhamah, and Lo-Ammi, signs of judgment on the house of Israel, with mercy still promised to the house of Judah. After Lo-Ammi is named, the word turns to promise: the children of Israel will be as the sand of the sea, and in the place where they were told they were not his people they will be called sons of the living God; Judah and Israel will be gathered together under one head, and the day of Jezreel will be great. In Hebrew Bibles, English Hosea 1:10–11 are Hosea 2:1–2. The numbers in this passage follow the WEB.

verses.text: The LORD’s word that came to Hosea the son of Beeri, in the days of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, kings of Judah, and in the days of Jeroboam the son of Joash, king of Israel.
verses.arminianNotes:
“The LORD’s word that came to Hosea the son of Beeri,” The book opens by naming the prophet and the kings of his days: Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah in Judah, and Jeroboam the son of Joash in Israel. The heading is a real historical frame for a word that came to a man in those reigns.

Arminian readers take the coming of the word as a genuine address, spoken in time to Hosea, a prophet who will now have to live the message he is sent to bear.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the same heading as the LORD’s own initiative: the word comes, the prophet is named, and the reigns are fixed by God’s timing.

Shared ground: the speaker of the book is the LORD, and the word comes to Hosea son of Beeri in the days of those kings. The traditions begin together.

verses.text: When the LORD spoke at first by Hosea, the LORD said to Hosea, “Go, take for yourself a wife of prostitution and children of unfaithfulness; for the land commits great adultery, forsaking the LORD.”
verses.arminianNotes:
When the LORD spoke at first by Hosea, he said, “Go, take for yourself a wife of prostitution and children of unfaithfulness; for the land commits great adultery, forsaking the LORD.” The marriage is a sign-act, and the reason is given in the same breath: the land itself is unfaithful, forsaking the LORD. Whether Gomer’s unfaithfulness had already begun before the marriage is more than the command itself states.

Arminian readers hear a costly, real command to the prophet, a living picture of the LORD’s faithful love toward a people who have turned from him, and a word the land can still recognize as about its own forsaking.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the same command as the LORD’s appointed sign, the prophet’s household taken up into the word that judges the land’s adultery.

Shared ground: the marriage figures the land’s unfaithfulness to the LORD. The imagery is a marriage, told in these words and not enlarged.

verses.text: So he went and took Gomer the daughter of Diblaim; and she conceived, and bore him a son.
verses.arminianNotes:
“So he went and took Gomer the daughter of Diblaim; and she conceived, and bore him a son.” Hosea obeys. Gomer is named, and her father Diblaim is named, and the first child is born to Hosea: “bore him a son.” The narrative is spare, and it does not say more about her.

Arminian readers hear a prophet who actually takes the wife he was sent to take, and a first child born to him, the beginning of a family that will now carry the LORD’s signs in its names.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the same going, the taking of Gomer, and the birth of a son to Hosea as the LORD’s word taking flesh in the prophet’s house.

Shared ground: Gomer daughter of Diblaim is the wife named, and the first son is born to Hosea. The verse is a simple report, and it is enough.

verses.text: The LORD said to him, “Call his name Jezreel, for yet a little while, and I will avenge the blood of Jezreel on the house of Jehu, and will cause the kingdom of the house of Israel to cease.
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD said to Hosea, “Call his name Jezreel, for yet a little while, and I will avenge the blood of Jezreel on the house of Jehu, and will cause the kingdom of the house of Israel to cease.” The child’s name is a place-name and a sentence: the blood of Jezreel will be avenged on Jehu’s house, and Israel’s kingdom will end. 2 Kings 9–10 records Jehu’s acts in Jezreel; this verse announces vengeance on that house and the end of the northern kingdom, and the two accounts are not blended.

Arminian readers hear a named judgment, soon to come, a moral accounting for blood already shed, and a word Israel can still hear as the LORD’s warning.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the naming, the vengeance on Jehu’s house, and the ending of Israel’s kingdom as the LORD’s own appointed word, sure in its timing.

Shared ground: the boy is Jezreel, and the LORD will avenge the blood of Jezreel and end the kingdom of Israel. 2 Kings 9–10 stands beside the verse by reference.

verses.text: It will happen in that day that I will break the bow of Israel in the valley of Jezreel.”
verses.arminianNotes:
“It will happen in that day that I will break the bow of Israel in the valley of Jezreel.” The bow is Israel’s fighting strength, and it will be broken in the same valley that gave the child his name. The verse does not name the army that will do it.

Arminian readers hear a coming day in a real place, a breaking of Israel’s power that answers the blood already named, a judgment the people can still take to heart while the bow is not yet broken.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the breaking of the bow in the valley of Jezreel as the LORD’s own act in that day, the military face of the kingdom’s end already announced.

Shared ground: Israel’s bow will be broken in the valley of Jezreel. The place-name now holds both the child’s name and the coming defeat.

verses.text: She conceived again, and bore a daughter. Then he said to him, “Call her name Lo-Ruhamah, for I will no longer have mercy on the house of Israel, that I should in any way pardon them.
verses.arminianNotes:
She conceived again and bore a daughter, and Hosea is told, “Call her name Lo-Ruhamah, for I will no longer have mercy on the house of Israel,” and will not pardon them. The name marks a withdrawal of mercy from the northern kingdom. The first child was born “to him”; this birth is told without that phrase. Many readers still take the daughter as the couple’s child; the sign is the name the LORD gives, and the verse does not say more about her parentage.

Arminian readers hear a real withholding of mercy, a sentence the house of Israel can still hear as the LORD’s response to their forsaking, and a name that will live in the prophet’s house as a warning.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the naming of Lo-Ruhamah and the end of mercy and pardon toward the house of Israel as the LORD’s own settled word for that kingdom.

Shared ground: the girl is named Lo-Ruhamah because the LORD will no longer have mercy on the house of Israel. The name and the reason are given together.

verses.text: But I will have mercy on the house of Judah, and will save them by the LORD their God, and will not save them by bow, sword, battle, horses, or horsemen.”
verses.arminianNotes:
“But I will have mercy on the house of Judah, and will save them by the LORD their God, and will not save them by bow, sword, battle, horses, or horsemen.” Mercy withheld from Israel is still promised to Judah. Their salvation will be by the LORD their God, not by weapons. The verse does not narrate a later campaign.

Arminian readers hear a real distinction in the LORD’s dealings, mercy still held out to Judah, and a salvation that will not rest on military means, a promise Judah can trust as the LORD’s own deliverance.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the mercy on Judah, and the saving by the LORD their God rather than by bow or sword, as his own purpose, set beside the word against Israel.

Shared ground: Judah is promised mercy and a salvation that is the LORD’s, not the work of weapons. The contrast with Israel is the verse’s own contrast.

verses.text: Now when she had weaned Lo-Ruhamah, she conceived, and bore a son.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Now when she had weaned Lo-Ruhamah, she conceived, and bore a son.” Time passes in the household: the daughter is weaned, and another son is born. The report is again spare, without the “bore him” of the first birth, and without further comment on the mother or the child.

Arminian readers hear the ordinary pace of a family, weaning and conceiving, a third child given into a house already marked by the LORD’s names, a life the prophet actually lives between the words.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the weaning, the new conception, and the birth of a son as the LORD’s timing of the next sign, the household again made the bearer of the word.

Shared ground: after Lo-Ruhamah is weaned, a third child is born. The verse is a narrative link, and it does not add a new charge.

verses.text: He said, “Call his name Lo-Ammi, for you are not my people, and I will not be yours.
verses.arminianNotes:
Hosea is told, “Call his name Lo-Ammi, for you are not my people, and I will not be yours.” The third name is a covenant breach: they are not his people, and he will not be theirs. The sign is as grave as the first two, and it is spoken in the second person to the people themselves.

Arminian readers hear a real rupture, a people addressed as no longer his, a word that still comes to them as the LORD’s own voice and so still treats them as hearers of the sentence.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the name Lo-Ammi, and the word “you are not my people, and I will not be yours.” as the LORD’s own judgment on Israel’s standing.

Shared ground: the boy is Lo-Ammi, and the reason is that they are not his people. The traditions can share this as a word of judgment, without a new dispute over the children’s names.

verses.text: Yet the number of the children of Israel will be as the sand of the sea, which can’t be measured or counted; and it will come to pass that, in the place where it was said to them, ‘You are not my people,’ they will be called ‘sons of the living God.’
verses.arminianNotes:
“Yet the number of the children of Israel will be as the sand of the sea, which can’t be measured or counted; and it will come to pass that, in the place where it was said to them, ‘You are not my people,’ they will be called ‘sons of the living God.’” After Lo-Ammi, the word turns: the people will be countless, and the place of the old sentence will become the place of a new name. Romans 9:25–26 and 1 Peter 2:10 take up this language; see those passages. They stand beside Hosea’s promise to Israel and are not merged with it.

Arminian readers hear a genuine reversal held out to the same people who were just called “not my people,” a promised mercy as real as the judgment, and a future in which they are named sons of the living God.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the sand of the sea, the reversal of “You are not my people,” and the new name “sons of the living God” as the LORD’s own sure promise, his purpose running through judgment into restoration.

Shared ground: the “not my people” word is not the last word. Judgment and restoration both belong to the LORD’s speech in this chapter.

verses.text: The children of Judah and the children of Israel will be gathered together, and they will appoint themselves one head, and will go up from the land; for great will be the day of Jezreel.
verses.arminianNotes:
“The children of Judah and the children of Israel will be gathered together, and they will appoint themselves one head, and will go up from the land; for great will be the day of Jezreel.” Judah and Israel are gathered under one head, and they go up from the land; Jezreel’s day, once a day of breaking, will be great. The one head is not named in this verse. Hosea 3:5 will speak of David their king; that later word stands beside this gathering and is not the same sentence.

Arminian readers hear a real hope of reunion, a people appointing one head and going up, a great day that turns the valley’s name toward gathering rather than only toward the broken bow.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the gathering of Judah and Israel, the one head, the going up from the land, and the great day of Jezreel as the LORD’s own appointed restoration.

Shared ground: the divided kingdoms will be gathered, and Jezreel’s day will be great. The head is not identified in this verse.
